transcript:
Meeting header:
- Date: 2027-03-11
- Start: 16:00 UTC
- Duration: ~58 minutes
- Attendees: Alex Park (Redwood AE), Samir Patel (Redwood SE), Marta Lopez (Vesper Infra), Jon Reed (Vesper ML Eng), Priya Singh (Vesper Security)

Summary:
Quick technical deep dive to align on Private VPC egress design, PrivateLink termination, split-horizon DNS for cluster-local resolution, NAT sizing and hairpin/MTU pitfalls, plus a focused exploration of KV-cache warmup, batching behavior, and quantization tradeoffs for throughput. Goal: produce an actionable playbook and run a short pilot.

Topics covered:
- PrivateLink termination options (TCP vs TLS tunnel, SNI, MTLS)
- Egress path: NAT Gateway vs Egress Proxy vs VPC Endpoints
- Split-horizon DNS for service discovery and keeping KV-cache traffic local
- MTU fragmentation and impact on latency for long token responses
- KV cache warmup, prefix caching, and continuous batching implications
- Quantization profile impact on latency vs tail accuracy
- Operational rollouts and fallbacks (canary vs A/B, circuit-breaker)

Transcript:
[00:00] Alex Park: hey everyone, thanks for joining. we'll keep this tight, 45 to 60 minutes. quick intros. samir, you wanna kick off?
[00:12] Samir Patel: yeah sure. hi all, im Samir from Redwood infra, my focus is runtime and networking for private deployments, i'll walk through the playbook and then we can scope a pilot.
[00:24] Marta Lopez: Marta here, infra at Vesper. we run a mixed cloud footprint, want to keep inference traffic inside our VPC when possible and avoid cross-az egress.
[00:30] Jon Reed: Jon, ML eng. my worry is throughput during peak clinical batch jobs and keeping latency predictable for interactive features.
[00:37] Priya Singh: Priya, security. SOC2 and data residencia are big. also SAML/SSO for admin access and KMS for keys.
[00:45] Alex Park: perfect. Samir, slide one?
[00:52] Samir Patel: ok so first principle, we prefer PrivateLink termination in the customer's account in a small HA set of NLBs, terminate TLS with mutual TLS if required, and route directly to our runtime through private IPs. two main modes: 1) L4 pass-through with SNI based routing, 2) TLS termination in our private connector then mTLS to the runtime. pass-through keeps certs in customer land but adds complexity for cross-zone hit, termination centralizes certs.
[01:28] Marta Lopez: question — does pass-through break ipv6 or change MTU? we've seen frag on jumbo frames when NLB sits in front.
[01:36] Samir Patel: good call. pass-through can surface MTU issues because of extra headers; we recommend 1500 as default and avoid Jumbo frames across the NLB. we've seen a 5–12ms bump when fragmentation occurs on long token streams.
[01:49] Jon Reed: 5–12ms per request? that's scary at scale. is that per token or per response?
[01:55] Samir Patel: per response tail when payloads exceed a single packet. for typical 256-token responses it's small but for long generations you can see the window spike. that's why we suggest prefix-based KV cache to reduce response lengths for common continuations.
[02:10] Marta Lopez: ok. next is split-horizon DNS — we've had issues where egress to public model catalog endpoints leaked out. how do you ensure catalog lookups stay local?
[02:19] Samir Patel: we recommend adding private hosted zones that override the public model catalog names used by the runtime; essentially split-horizon so DNS for model.redwood.ai (example) resolves to 10.x.x.x inside the VPC. also we advocate for static routing for S3/backing stores via VPC endpoints to avoid NAT.
[02:34] Priya Singh: is there audit trail for those DNS overrides? we need to show in audits what was resolved.
[02:39] Alex Park: yes, our connector logs include DNS mappings and we can stream to CloudWatch/Stackdriver or the customer's logging plane. but if you need immutable audit trails we can push DNS query logs to S3 with retention.
[02:51] Jon Reed: switching to KV cache — can you explain warmup behavior? our workload has lots of short chat sessions then occasional long batch jobs.
[02:58] Samir Patel: KV cache is prefix-addressable; warmup is twofold: initial cache population when you run sampling prompts, and steady-state continuity where continuous batching keeps hot prefixes resident. recommended warmup: pre-seed cache with representative prompts (we can provide a script) and run a lightweight crawl for 1–2 hours prior to a pilot.
[03:19] Jon Reed: what about eviction policy? LRU?
[03:21] Samir Patel: it's an LRU with size-tiered buckets; large KV entries (long pastes) are demoted and thinned. you can pin keys for application-critical prefixes but that consumes memory. for most customers we keep ~12–18GB per GPU for KV cache which supports about Xk 256-token prefixes — optics differ by quantization and the model memory footprint.
[03:40] Marta Lopez: you said 'Xk' — can you quantify for our instance types? we run p4d-equivalent nodes.
[03:45] Samir Patel: for p4d-equivalent with q4f quant we typically see ~14GB usable for KV cache per GPU supporting ~24k 256-token prefix entries. with q3f or int8 you can push more but there's tail accuracy tradeoffs.
[03:58] Jon Reed: tail accuracy tradeoffs — can you repeat, we care about clinical correctness.
[04:02] Samir Patel: sure; lower-bit quant (int8/q3f) reduces per-token latency and memory pressure but can introduce subtle regression on rare tokens — for clinical text we recommend evaluation harness against your prompt set. Redwood Optimize can run a regression alert that maps metric drift to prompt buckets.
[04:20] Priya Singh: we need that in writing for compliance. also KMS integration — where are keys held in PrivateLink flow?
[04:26] Samir Patel: KMS keys stay in customer account if you run KMS-backed encryption at rest; our runtime supports using a customer-managed key via cross-account grant. we can demonstrate the policy during the pilot.
[04:36] Alex Park: ok moving on to egress patterns — NAT gateway limits are a common bottleneck. Marta, any constraints?
[04:43] Marta Lopez: our NAT gateways are shared and have port exhaustion limits during spikes; we hit ephemeral port saturation last year.
[04:50] Samir Patel: recommended pattern: use VPC endpoints for all static traffic (S3, ECR) and reserve NAT for dynamic control-plane calls. For customer to Redwood PrivateLink traffic, we prefer direct PrivateLink so NAT is bypassed. If you must route via NAT (legacy), we use connection pooling and keep-alive to reduce ephemeral churn. also consider using egress proxy (squid/priv) inside a subnet with higher port capacity and health-checks.
[05:16] Jon Reed: connection pooling — does the runtime reuse HTTP/2 channels for streaming?
[05:21] Samir Patel: yes, our runtime uses HTTP/2 multiplexing with pinned channels per connection; but when you front with an egress proxy you need to ensure it supports HTTP/2 pass-through, otherwise you lose multiplexing benefits which impacts throughput.
[05:33] Marta Lopez: about hairpin NAT — sometimes VMs in same AZ route out to the NAT and back in causing hairpin. we found TTL issues and odd connection resets.
[05:41] Samir Patel: hairpin is a known anti-pattern. recommended is to use local resolver that routes PrivateLink ranges to ENIs — avoid hairpin by keeping the right route table entries and use target-based routing if supported.
[05:53] Alex Park: we should call out MTU test steps — Samir?
[05:56] Samir Patel: yeah quick checklist: 1) set instance MTU to 1500, 2) test ICMP path MTU to private link endpoint, 3) generate 4kB responses to verify no fragmentation, 4) if fragmentation occurs add MSS clamping on the NLB or use TCP MSS clamp on your gateway. we'll share a script.
[06:17] Priya Singh: for the audit we also need a mitigation for intermittent TLS renegotiation failures. we've seen some clients where cert rotation caused 502s.
[06:26] Samir Patel: for cert rotation we recommend rolling cert rotation with canary and keep a temp fallback to a hosted regional model variant. death by 502 is usually because the NLB was caching a dead backend; we set probe intervals and a graceful drain of 30s to avoid in-flight generation drops.
[06:41] Jon Reed: can we talk throughput numbers — baseline per-GPU tokens/s with batching and with cache?
[06:46] Samir Patel: bench numbers vary by model. for a 7B family model on A100-equivalent with q4f and continuous batching we typically see ~350–450 tokens/s raw; with KV hits and 64-request batching we can reach effective 1k tokens/s because many tokens are served from cache locally and batching amortizes kernel launch overhead. important caveat: tail latency for cold prefixes remains dominated by the model forward time.
[07:09] Jon Reed: and what about 99p latency?
[07:12] Samir Patel: 99p depends on queueing; with autoscale config to keep queue depth under the SLO, we have seen 99p around 120–180ms for these configs, but again long generations can be seconds. the playbook's batching policy is conservative for interactive paths.
[07:27] Marta Lopez: autoscale — do you recommend burst pools? we want predictable latency but also cost control.
[07:32] Samir Patel: yes dedicated reserved pool with a small burst capacity is the common pattern. set a strict scale-down delay (90–120s) and a canary fallback to a smaller cheaper model when capacity is exhausted.
[07:44] Alex Park: practical question — how do we instrument KV cache hit-rate and attribute to customer requests?
[07:50] Samir Patel: runtime emits per-request headers: X-Runtime-KV-Hit:true/false, and aggregated metrics in Prometheus format. we'll push the exporter into your observability plane. those metrics include hit-rate by prefix hash, eviction events, and pin counts.
[08:04] Jon Reed: can we get an alert when hit-rate drops below X%?
[08:07] Samir Patel: yes, we can pre-configure a PagerDuty rule; Redwood Console supports threshold and regression alerts.
[08:12] Marta Lopez: troubleshooting scenario — we have sporadic 503s post-deploy. what's your runbook?
[08:18] Samir Patel: first check NLB target health and connection counts, then check NAT port exhaustion, then KV cache OOM or backend OOMs. we also look at the runtime's trace ids and tail logs for OOM or CUDA kernel failures. often it's a mix of bad autoscale policy and an NLB health-probe mismatch.
[08:35] Alex Park: can we run a short simulation during the pilot that exercises NAT port saturation?
[08:38] Marta Lopez: yes, we can spin up a synthetic load generator.
[08:41] Samir Patel: great — plan: 24h pilot, start with small traffic, seed KV cache, run a synthetic ramp to emulate spike, capture metrics.
[08:50] Priya Singh: security — quick checklist: SAML for admin, KMS for keys, RBAC audit logs, network ACLs, assured egress endpoints. do you support FIPS TLS?
[08:59] Samir Patel: we support FIPS cipher suites in the connector; we can enable that for PrivateLink. for KMS, we can use customer-managed keys. RBAC maps to your SSO groups via SCIM if required.
[09:12] Jon Reed: one more question on quantization — is there a recommended quant profile for clinical NER tasks?
[09:18] Samir Patel: for NER we generally recommend q4f for minimal regression, q3f for cost-sensitive cases after running the evaluation harness. we'll run a small A/B with your annotated dataset.
[09:29] Marta Lopez: ok wrapping up — let's enumerate the exact pilot steps and owners.
[09:33] Alex Park: Samir, can you shard that into a playbook?
[09:36] Samir Patel: yes i'll produce a playbook with sections: networking checklist (routes, privatelink, MTU, NAT), KV-cache warmup script and sizing, batching config examples (target batch size, latency SLO mapping), quantization evaluation steps, observability dashboards, and rollback plan.
[09:50] Marta Lopez: timeline? we can start pilot early next week.
[09:53] Alex Park: Samir will share docs by Friday (03/13), Marta will give subnets by 03/16; Samir + Marta will kick off pilot 03/20 for 24–48h. Priya will vet compliance docs by 03/15.
[10:06] Jon Reed: quick technical nit — when you describe prefix pinning, what is the CPU overhead for pin management?
[10:11] Samir Patel: pin management is lightweight, it's a small metadata map; CPU overhead is negligible compared to GPU inference but it increments the memory footprint. pinning thousands of keys is not recommended unless you need deterministic hit rates.
[10:24] Marta Lopez: are there any gotchas with the cloud provider's PrivateLink quotas? some providers limit the number of endpoints per account.
[10:31] Samir Patel: yes, quota limits exist. for big pilots we'll request quota bump proactively. we'll include quota guidance in the playbook.
[10:40] Priya Singh: will you include an encrypted log-forwarding config example? we need to ensure PII isn't logged.
[10:46] Samir Patel: absolutely — we'll show scrubbing rules, masking and redaction options, plus a log-sampling config so raw prompt text doesn't get persisted unless explicitly allowed.
[10:55] Alex Park: ok final recap and next steps — can we list them out?
[10:59] Samir Patel: sure — 1) share PrivateLink/networking playbook (Samir, due 03/13) 2) Vesper to share subnet/CIDR and NAT details (Marta, due 03/16) 3) run KV-cache warmup & perf test (Samir/Marta, due 03/18) 4) schedule onsite/on-prem throughput test with Jon & Alex (target week of 03/22) 5) Priya to review security pack (Priya, due 03/15).
[11:28] Marta Lopez: sounds good, thanks everyone.
[11:31] Alex Park: thanks all — we'll follow up in email with links to the scripts and the pilot plan.
